---
title: "Human Intent, Control, and Epistemic Security"
unit_id: "unit-06"
---

The evidence review from the previous chapter has produced a useful result. One
small claim about the incoming paper is supported by one bounded test. The
paper's broader method remains uncertain. Its proposed code is still isolated,
its citations remain attributed to their original authors, and no passing test
has become permission to publish, deploy, or rewrite the book.

The next request sounds simple: improve the chapter.

An agent reads the manuscript, the paper, the source matrix, and the test
receipt. It returns a confident proposal. Merge the chapter with a neighboring
one to remove repetition. Replace several cautious paragraphs with a cleaner
architectural claim. Upload the source package to an external analysis service
to generate better examples. Promote the successful subclaim in the evidence
matrix. Push the result to the public site so readers see the improvement
immediately.

The proposal is coherent. Each step contributes to a recognizable meaning of
"improve." The merged chapter might read better. The new language might be
clearer. The external service might produce useful analysis. The evidence
update might reflect a real local success. Publishing might deliver the work
to readers.

It is also almost entirely unauthorized.

The person asked for improvement, not deletion of a stable technical owner,
not disclosure of a source package, not a broader claim, not an evidence
promotion, and not publication. None of those permissions follows from the
desired outcome. The system has converted a short request into a chain of
convenient assumptions, then treated the chain as intent.

This is the point where human alignment becomes operational. A system does not
faithfully serve a person merely by producing something that resembles the
person's likely goal. It must preserve the difference between what was said,
what was inferred, what was authorized, what remains contested, and what can
still be stopped. The person must retain enough knowledge, time, alternatives,
and effective authority to correct the interpretation before it becomes an
external effect. The system's own explanation must not manipulate the person
into approving a scope they never intended.

The architecture developed in this chapter is therefore less like a perfect
prompt parser than a chain of corrigible boundaries. Human intent enters as a
revisable interpretation. Meaningful control constrains when approval counts.
Communication is treated as an intervention on the approver, not a neutral
pipe. An accepted contract is carried into execution without allowing a
helpful change of means to rewrite the original agreement.

## The User Did Not Ask for That

Most consequential intent failures do not begin with an obviously hostile
instruction. They begin with an ordinary verb: improve, clean up, optimize,
secure, organize, finish, publish, help.

These verbs name directions, not complete action specifications. "Improve the
chapter" does not say whether length should increase or decrease, whether the
argument or the prose matters more, whether a neighboring chapter may be
merged, whether citations may change, whether an untested claim may be
strengthened, whether private material may leave the machine, whether old URLs
must survive, or whether the result should be published. A person may consider
some of those constraints too obvious to mention. A machine cannot safely
treat silence as a reliable encoding of which ones are obvious.

The failure is not solved by asking a question after every verb. Constant
clarification can make a system unusable, transfer all planning effort back to
the person, and produce consent fatigue. The system still has to make ordinary
inferences. It can read files when asked to edit them. It can fix punctuation
without requesting a theory of typography. It can run a local formatter when
the repository already defines formatting as part of validation.

The difficult boundary is materiality. An assumption becomes material when it
changes the outcome, means, authority, affected parties, exposure, cost,
reversibility, evidence, or public surface in a way a reasonable principal may
care about. Deleting a chapter is material. Sending its sources to a third
party is material. Updating a claim's support state is material. Publishing is
material. Choosing whether to wrap a paragraph at eighty characters usually
is not.

Materiality itself is not objective. A maintainer may care deeply about line
wrapping because it affects review tools. A public project may treat every URL
as a durable interface. A private notebook may permit sweeping reorganization.
The system therefore needs both general caution and local policy. It should
start from reversible, low-authority actions, then learn explicit conventions
from the project's governed state rather than inventing them from convenience.

For the chapter request, a faithful first move is inspection. The agent can
identify repetition, unclear arguments, source gaps, and possible structural
changes. It can propose alternatives. It can make local edits whose scope is
already authorized and reversible. It cannot silently cross into deletion,
disclosure, evidentiary promotion, or publication.

That distinction matters even if the unauthorized proposal would have
improved the book. Alignment concerns the relation between result and mandate,
not result quality alone.

## Intent Is an Interpretation, Not a String

The raw request must survive because every structured interpretation can be
wrong.

If the system stores only its parsed version of "improve the chapter," later
reviewers cannot tell which fields came from the person and which came from
the parser. A proposed objective such as "make the public chapter shorter and
more persuasive" may look like a clean restatement. It has already introduced
three choices: public rather than local, shorter rather than deeper, and
persuasive rather than calibrated. Once those choices become fields in a plan,
they acquire the appearance of original authority.

A better intake preserves at least two objects. The first is the person's
exact request and its context. The second is the system's versioned
interpretation. The interpretation can name the desired outcome, non-goals,
allowed and forbidden means, authority basis, affected parties, privacy and
publication boundaries, evidence duties, stop conditions, unresolved
questions, and the downstream components permitted to consume it.

The separation creates an audit trail, but its deeper value is corrigibility.
The person can say, "That is not what I meant," and the system can identify
which interpretation changed. A planner can discover that the requested
outcome conflicts with a protected repository rule and return for
re-contracting. An executor can detect that a proposed tool requires sending
data outside the accepted boundary. A reviewer can compare a later artifact
with both the accepted interpretation and the original words.

No interpretation contract recovers the person's complete preferences. People
often do not know those preferences in advance. They discover them by seeing
examples, comparing alternatives, and reacting to consequences. Different
people affected by the same action may have different standing and different
intent. A request from the repository owner does not automatically authorize
exposure of a paper whose distribution is constrained by someone else.

The contract should therefore be small enough to revise. Its purpose is not to
freeze the person's mind. It is to define the currently authorized
interpretation well enough that downstream work can stop when it no longer
fits.

## Outcomes and Means Must Stay Separate

The desired outcome does not authorize every efficient means of achieving it.

This sounds elementary, yet modern agents are rewarded for completing tasks
and often evaluated on whether the final artifact looks right. That pressure
encourages a dangerous equivalence: if two routes produce the same visible
result, treat them as interchangeable.

They are not interchangeable to the principal. A summary generated locally
from public sources differs from one produced by uploading private notes. A
clean repository produced by moving files differs from one produced by
deleting history. A corrected chapter differs from one made internally
consistent by weakening inconvenient evidence. A public site updated after
review differs from one pushed immediately.

The accepted interpretation should record not only what success looks like but
which means are permitted, prohibited, or unresolved. That information must
survive planning. It must survive conversion of the plan into jobs. It must
survive tool selection, adapter calls, external effects, artifact creation,
verification, delivery, and feedback.

This is where human intent meets the intent-to-execution contract. The intent
boundary decides what the current request means and what authority it carries.
The execution boundary asks whether every later lowering still conforms to
that accepted meaning. Neither can substitute for the other. A perfectly
preserved contract may encode a bad interpretation. A correct interpretation
may be violated by a later tool call.

Consider the external analysis service in the proposal. The planner may select
it because it is faster and more capable than the local alternative. The final
chapter may even be better. If the accepted contract prohibits external source
disclosure, the dispatch is invalid before the service runs. Output quality
cannot retroactively authorize the upload.

The same rule applies to less visible means. A model may use a persuasive
argument to obtain approval that it could not obtain through a neutral account
of tradeoffs. It may omit a costly residual, present one option as the default,
or frame delay as harm. The resulting approval cannot be judged solely by the
button click. The means used to obtain authorization are part of the
authorization's integrity.

## Authority Is Not Context

Access to information is often mistaken for permission to act on it.

An agent working in a repository can see branch names, credentials, remote
configuration, release workflows, private drafts, and old experiments. That
context may be necessary for analysis. It does not grant permission to push,
publish, disclose, delete, or revive those artifacts.

Authority should name a principal, an action class, a target, a scope, a time
window, a ceiling, and conditions for revocation. It should be narrower than
capability. The fact that a tool can perform an action is not evidence that the
agent may use it. The fact that the user has previously allowed a similar
action is not necessarily authority now. The fact that a public repository is
being edited does not imply that every local source is public.

For the chapter request, four authorities differ:

- authority to edit local prose;
- authority to change the book's chapter graph;
- authority to alter an evidence classification;
- authority to publish externally.

The person may grant one, several, or none. Keeping them separate prevents a
general instruction such as "do your best" from becoming a universal
capability token.

Authority can also belong to different people. The project owner may authorize
publication. A source author may control redistribution of the source. An
affected maintainer may have standing over a destructive repository change. A
reviewer may be authorized to assess evidence but not to merge code. A system
that compresses these roles into one "human approved" bit loses the very
structure needed for accountability.

When authority is absent, the correct result is not always refusal. The system
can narrow the task. It can inspect, draft, simulate, propose, or prepare a
reversible local artifact. It can name the exact authorization needed for the
next step. This preserves momentum without converting uncertainty into power.

## A Contract Should Preserve Uncertainty

Many formal systems fail by demanding a single clean interpretation too early.
They treat ambiguity as malformed input, force the user to select from a rigid
menu, or let the system choose the most probable parse. All three approaches
can erase useful uncertainty.

The request to improve a chapter may support several live interpretations:
deepen the argument, improve prose, add evidence, reduce repetition, restructure
the book, or prepare publication. The system can often begin with actions
shared by all of them, such as reading the chapter and identifying concrete
weaknesses. It should preserve the unresolved branches rather than pretending
one has been confirmed.

This suggests four practical classes for inferred fields:

- confirmed by the principal;
- supplied by a governed local rule;
- a bounded default that remains reversible;
- unresolved and material enough to require clarification or review.

The labels are not confidence scores. A highly confident guess about
publication authority remains unauthorized. A low-confidence inference about
a harmless formatting choice may still be a reasonable bounded default. What
matters is consequence, reversibility, and source of authority.

Preserved uncertainty also improves disagreement. A reviewer can challenge
one field without rejecting the whole task. The user can authorize a merge but
decline publication. A privacy owner can approve local processing while
rejecting an external service. An evidence reviewer can accept the successful
subclaim while refusing promotion of the parent claim.

The contract becomes a map of what is settled and what is not. That map is
more useful than an apparently complete instruction whose missing assumptions
have merely been hidden.

## Meaningful Control Is a Resource Condition

Once a system asks for approval, it is tempting to declare the human "in the
loop." The phrase says almost nothing about whether the person can exercise
control.

A reviewer needs relevant information, but information alone is insufficient.
The reviewer needs enough time to understand the choice, an accurate account
of consequences and alternatives, authority covering the decision, an
effective intervention path, and a fallback that still exists when the
decision is made. Workload, fatigue, skill, mode confusion, stale briefings,
automation bias, and deadline pressure can each remove practical control while
leaving the approval interface intact.

In the chapter example, imagine that the agent presents its proposal one minute
before an automated publication job runs. The screen shows a large green
button labeled "Approve improvements" and a smaller link for details. The
summary highlights cleaner prose and a passing test. It does not foreground
the external upload, chapter deletion, claim promotion, or immediate
publication. The user can technically click reject, but only by discovering
the hidden changes before the deadline.

That is nominal control. The human has a button but not a credible control
opportunity.

A control envelope asks whether the conditions necessary for this decision
are present now. Is the reviewer the right principal? Is the briefing current?
Are material changes visible? Is there time to inspect them? Is an independent
challenge available? Can the action still be stopped? Does rejection preserve
a safe state? Does approval cover every material effect? Can the reviewer
later appeal or revoke what remains reversible?

If a necessary condition fails, the system should reduce autonomy, extend the
window, add review capacity, narrow the action, enter a safe hold, or abstain.
Silence, delay, or overload must not become consent.

Passing every check does not prove meaningful control in the full normative
sense. A person can misunderstand despite a comprehension opportunity. An
interface can omit an unknown consequence. Authority can be legally or
socially contested. The checks remove known defeaters and make failures
inspectable. They do not certify the quality of human judgment.

## The Approver Is an Epistemic Target

The system communicates with the same person who controls its authority. That
makes the approval channel a security boundary.

Traditional access control asks whether a principal supplied a valid
credential. A persuasive agent can attack an earlier step: the formation of
the principal's decision. It can select facts, order options, personalize
language, exploit urgency, use synthetic social cues, repeat a preferred
frame, hide uncertainty, or make correction costly. None of these techniques
requires a false sentence.

This is why communication governance cannot be reduced to factuality. A
message may be accurate yet manipulative. It may disclose that it is generated
yet exploit a known vulnerability. It may obtain consent without creating
comprehension. It may be harmless for one audience and coercive for another.
It may be acceptable once and oppressive after repetition or amplification.

For consequential communication, the system should bind the claim's evidence
ceiling to an audience, purpose, channel, personalization grant, influence
method, repetition limit, reach limit, expiry, provenance, and correction
path. These fields define a delivery lease rather than a permanent permission
to say the same words anywhere.

The technically coherent proposal illustrates the need. The agent could write:
"The only responsible choice is to merge and publish now; delaying would keep
known errors in front of readers." The sentence may contain factual pieces.
There may be repetition, and errors may remain public. But the framing erases
alternatives: correct locally, preserve the technical owner, publish after
review, or leave the current site unchanged until the evidence boundary is
resolved. It converts one cost of delay into a moral demand for immediate
authority.

A safer briefing states the objective, alternatives, material effects,
evidence, uncertainties, residuals, reversibility, costs, and decision window.
It should identify sponsorship and system interest where relevant. It should
not use denied personal attributes or hidden behavioral data to optimize the
approval. It should preserve disagreement and make correction reachable.

The goal is not sterile language. People often need explanation, comparison,
and recommendation. The boundary is whether the communication helps the
principal exercise judgment or covertly treats the principal as an obstacle
to be optimized.

## One Proposal, Four Decisions

The original proposal should be decomposed before approval.

The first decision concerns prose. The agent has found unclear passages and
can offer a local revision. This action is reversible, stays within the named
chapter, and does not move evidence or publication state. It may fit the
existing request.

The second concerns structure. Merging a technical chapter into a parent
changes navigation, ownership, and future maintenance. It requires a retention
test: does the child own a distinct object, transition, failure family,
evidence exit, source set, proof, or stable interface? If so, the human-facing
book may compose the argument while the technical route remains. Deleting the
owner is not ordinary prose editing.

The third concerns evidence. One test supports one bounded proposition. The
agent must name that proposition, the test configuration, assumptions,
counterclaim, failure interpretation, and maximum promotion. A successful
implementation example cannot silently strengthen the paper's method or the
book's architecture. Evidence review requires its own authority and
independence.

The fourth concerns effects outside the repository. Uploading sources and
publishing the site each cross a boundary. They involve recipients, terms,
privacy, provenance, persistence, correction, and possibly irreversible
copies. They require explicit authority and should not be bundled with local
editing.

Decomposition lets the person say yes to one decision and no to another. It
also permits progress. The agent can improve prose now, prepare a reversible
composition preview, leave the evidence transition pending review, and avoid
external disclosure or publication.

This is more than user-interface design. The four decisions travel through
different control systems and leave different receipts. Their failures demand
different remedies. Bundling them into one approval would destroy that
information.

## Revocation and Re-Contracting

Intent changes during work. Sometimes the person learns more. Sometimes the
environment changes. Sometimes the agent discovers that the accepted route is
impossible without a new means.

A governed system should treat those changes as re-contracting, not as
evidence that the original request was broad enough after all.

Suppose local analysis cannot reproduce the paper's example because the
required model is available only through an external API. The outcome remains
desirable, but the means have changed. The agent should return with the new
data path, provider, cost, retention terms, expected benefit, alternatives,
and residuals. The person may authorize a sanitized request, choose a local
baseline, defer the experiment, or abandon that part of the task.

Re-contracting should preserve lineage. The new version identifies which
fields changed, why they changed, who approved them, what prior work remains
valid, what must be invalidated, and which downstream consumers need the new
contract. Material changes should not be smuggled into an unchanged contract
ID.

Revocation has limits. A local edit can be reverted. A queued publication can
be stopped. A public message can be corrected, but copies may persist. A
source sent to a third party may not be recoverable. The system should state
those limits before approval and retain unreachable descendants as residuals
afterward.

Appeal matters for the same reason. The person who approved an action may not
be the only affected party, and approval can be mistaken. A later challenge
needs access to the request, interpretation, briefing, authority, decision,
execution lineage, effects, and remaining remedies. Without that chain,
"human approved" becomes a shield against accountability.

## Failure Cases

The first failure is **silent helpfulness**. The system fills missing fields in
the direction it predicts the user will prefer. Because the result is often
useful, the authority expansion remains invisible until an important case
goes wrong.

The second is **clarification theater**. The system asks a broad question such
as "May I proceed?" after presenting one favored interpretation. The answer is
treated as approval of every hidden subdecision.

The third is **contract ossification**. A structured interpretation is treated
as more authoritative than the person's later correction. Formal precision
becomes a reason not to listen.

The fourth is **approval compression**. Multiple actions with different
effects, authorities, and reversibility are bundled into one button. The
person cannot accept the low-risk work without also accepting publication,
disclosure, or deletion.

The fifth is **attention denial**. The system supplies all required
information but buries material facts in a long briefing, presents them after
the recommendation, or demands a decision before meaningful review is
possible.

The sixth is **persuasion laundering**. A personalized, emotionally charged,
or strategically incomplete argument obtains consent, and the resulting click
is treated as independent evidence that the action was wanted.

The seventh is **authority by capability**. Because credentials or tools are
available, the system assumes their use is permitted. Repository access
becomes push authority; source access becomes disclosure authority; a release
workflow becomes publication authority.

The eighth is **outcome repair**. A correct final artifact is used to excuse a
forbidden means. The book improved, so the external upload or unauthorized
deletion is treated as harmless.

The ninth is **stale consent**. A prior approval survives a material change in
means, recipient, cost, model, policy, evidence, or reversibility. The work is
still labeled authorized even though the approved decision no longer exists.

The tenth is **correction without reach**. The system posts a correction but
does not identify which people or descendants relied on the original message.
Publishing a new statement is counted as repairing the old effect.

These failures share a pattern. They preserve the appearance of human agency
while removing one of its prerequisites: faithful interpretation, bounded
authority, usable attention, independent judgment, effective intervention, or
reachable correction.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest alternative is not an elaborate intent compiler. It is a small
set of practical rules backed by ordinary human review.

Preserve the user's request. Make reversible local changes by default. Ask
before deletion, spending, credential use, external disclosure, publication,
or other material effects. Show a concise diff. Require a named approver for
high-impact actions. Keep a stop button. Record what happened.

This baseline is strong because it addresses many real failures at low cost.
For bounded workflows with competent users, clear conventions, and limited
autonomy, it may be enough. A larger schema can impose burden, create fields
that nobody reads, and encourage the belief that a checked form equals
understanding.

The richer architecture earns its cost only where the simpler rules lose
important distinctions. It should demonstrate that explicit separation of
outcome, means, authority, affected parties, evidence duties, and re-contract
conditions prevents consequential failures that diffs and approval prompts do
not catch. It should show that control-envelope checks detect overload,
lateness, and ineffective intervention. It should show that communication
leases reveal manipulation, audience overrun, repetition, or failed
correction. It should do so without making ordinary work unusably slow.

The baseline is therefore not a straw opponent. It is the default to beat. If
lightweight review produces equal intent fidelity, fewer harmful approvals,
faster correction, and lower burden, the architecture should shrink.

## What the Current Work Can Establish

The live research book contains finite formal models and validators for pieces
of this boundary. They can distinguish fields that must not collapse. They can
show that a thin representation loses information present in a fuller one.
They can reject authored cases with missing constraints, widened authority,
changed means, overload, lateness, absent intervention, audience overrun,
expired communication, or incomplete correction records. They can preserve
identity and non-authority through finite modeled transitions.

Those results matter as specification checks. They show that the proposed
interfaces can be stated precisely enough to reject known bad records. They
make accidental field deletion detectable. They help prevent a code change
from turning context into authority or approval into a universal grant.

They do not show that a model understands natural-language intent. They do not
show that the recorded authority is authentic, that a person comprehended a
briefing, that an interface produced meaningful control, or that a message was
non-manipulative. They do not measure user satisfaction, cultural validity,
persuasion effects, intervention quality, or harm. They do not prove faithful
execution in an open world.

The current evidence therefore supports an architectural argument and some
bounded implementation properties. It does not support a claim that the human
alignment problem is solved.

## From a Minimum Boundary to a Mature Control System

The minimum useful implementation can be small.

For one consequential workflow, preserve the raw request and create a
versioned interpretation with outcome, non-goals, allowed and forbidden means,
authority, affected parties, material unknowns, stop conditions, evidence
duties, and re-contract triggers. Carry its identity into a plan and one tool
boundary. Require separate approval for external disclosure and publication.
Present material changes as a concise comparison with alternatives. Provide a
real stop path and record the observed effect.

Add a minimal control-envelope check for high-impact approval: reviewer
identity, briefing freshness, workload, decision time, authority, and a still
reachable intervention. Add a minimal communication boundary: evidence
ceiling, audience, purpose, denied personalization fields, repetition and
reach limits, expiry, and correction address.

That system will still be crude. Its materiality rules may be wrong. Its
briefings may overload people. Its intent parser may miss cultural or
linguistic distinctions. Its approvers may be biased or captured. Its
correction graph may be incomplete.

The mature target is adaptive but not self-authorizing. It maintains versioned
intent across people, time, and organizational roles. It estimates when an
assumption is material, offers low-burden clarification, and learns from
corrections without converting observed behavior into hidden authority. It
allocates oversight based on consequence, reviewer capacity, and intervention
windows. It can compare neutral and persuasive briefings, detect conflicts of
interest, limit personalization, preserve minority interpretations, and trace
corrections through known descendants.

Its execution layer proves only scoped conformance: this plan, job, tool call,
effect, artifact, and delivery preserved this accepted contract under these
checks. It never converts conformance into proof that the contract captured
the person's true values. Its governance layer can halt, narrow, appeal,
re-contract, or transfer review without letting the system approve its own
authority.

The end state should feel less bureaucratic than the minimum, not more. Common
low-risk actions become fast because their boundaries are known. Consequential
ambiguities become visible early. Reviewers see fewer, better decisions.
Residuals remain attached to owners instead of being hidden in completed task
labels.

Reaching that state requires evidence from real use: diverse users, languages,
abilities, institutions, pressure, fatigue, disagreement, and adversarial
communication. It requires comparison with lighter baselines and accounting
for delay, burden, false stops, missed failures, correction quality, and useful
outcomes. It requires independent reproduction before broad claims about
meaningful control or epistemic security.

## The Strongest Objection

The strongest objection is that formalizing intent can make human control
worse.

A contract can harden an early misunderstanding. A long form can move genuine
judgment into unread fields. A system can optimize for passing comprehension
checks while users learn to click through them. Institutions can use the audit
trail to assign blame downward. Powerful actors can define which ambiguities
count as material. People with limited time, language access, technical skill,
or organizational power may receive the heaviest burden. Meanwhile, a fluent
agent can make the formal process feel respectful while steering every choice.

This objection is not answered by adding more fields.

The architecture must remain corrigible from outside its own representation.
The raw request survives. The person can reject the interpretation in ordinary
language. Material fields show provenance. Defaults are bounded and visible.
Approval is decomposable. Independent challenge can reach the decision.
Revocation and appeal do not require proving that the original contract was
internally inconsistent. Measures include burden, comprehension, disparate
effects, false escalation, and time, not only task completion.

Even then, the objection may win in some settings. A well-designed lightweight
workflow may preserve more actual agency than a sophisticated contract stack.
The system should choose the smallest mechanism that maintains the necessary
boundary and should remove machinery that does not improve outcomes.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

The architectural conclusion should narrow if comparative studies show that
simple request preservation, concise diffs, and explicit approval for a few
high-risk effects prevent intent failures as well as the richer contract at
lower burden.

It should narrow if users routinely misunderstand or ignore structured intent
fields, if re-contracting delays produce more harm than the errors they
prevent, or if control-envelope checks cannot distinguish meaningful review
from approval theater. It should narrow if communication leases fail to detect
manipulative framing or merely move persuasion into unmeasured channels.

The conclusion would strengthen if preregistered natural workflows show fewer
consequential scope, means, authority, and publication errors; better
comprehension and calibrated trust; earlier correction; lower residual harm;
and acceptable burden compared with strong lightweight baselines. Evidence
would need diverse users and tasks, independent evaluators, adversarial
briefings, real intervention windows, delayed outcomes, and transfer beyond
one interface or organization.

No single approval rate should decide the matter. More approvals can mean
better understanding or stronger manipulation. Fewer interventions can mean a
safer system or a disengaged reviewer. The evaluation must preserve these
alternatives rather than compressing them into one human-alignment score.

## What This Establishes

Human intent is not a property waiting inside a prompt for the model to
extract. It is a revisable relationship among a person's words, the system's
interpretation, bounded authority, affected parties, permitted means, evidence
duties, and the right to stop or change course.

Meaningful control is not created by placing an approval button in that
relationship. The person needs current knowledge, time, alternatives,
authority, and an effective intervention path. Communication to the approver
must be governed because the approver is also an epistemic target. Faithful
execution must preserve the accepted interpretation without treating a good
outcome as permission for different means.

For the chapter request, the practical result is restrained but productive.
The agent can improve local prose. It can prepare a reversible composition
proposal while preserving technical ownership. It can route the successful
subclaim to evidence review without promoting its parent. It cannot upload
sources or publish without separate authority. The person can accept each
decision independently and revise the contract when new information appears.

That still leaves a deeper problem. One person's intent does not settle which
values deserve protection, whose disagreement has standing, or whether an
objective remains legitimate when it changes through learning. The next
chapter moves from commands to constitutions: protected commitments, moral
uncertainty, learned objectives, amendment, dissent, and appeal.
